analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes outright.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on February 12, 1997, and never advanced further or received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would eliminate the federal estate tax, gift tax, and generation-skipping transfer tax, which apply only to very large wealth transfers. Repeal would apply to estates of people dying after enactment. The bill attracted one cosponsor, was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, and received no further action for the remainder of the 105th Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to very large estates — the wealthiest households — would gain the most, since the estate tax applies only to large inheritances; very wealthy families would no longer face tax on transfers of farms, businesses, and investment wealth at death.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the estate tax entirely for decedents dying after enactment, so no estate would owe federal estate tax regardless of size.
Repeals the gift tax and generation-skipping transfer tax, ending federal tax on lifetime large gifts and transfers that skip a generation.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury — and ultimately taxpayers generally — would bear the cost of lost revenue, since these taxes fall almost entirely on very large estates and gifts.

drawbacks.text: The estate tax applies only to the largest estates, so repeal delivers its benefits exclusively to heirs of the wealthiest families while reducing federal revenue used to fund government programs.
An immediate full repeal would concentrate inherited wealth further, since heirs of the largest fortunes would pay nothing on transfers that are currently taxed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits flow to a narrow group — heirs of the largest estates — while the cost is broad, in the form of lost federal revenue. For ordinary working people the bill offers no direct benefit.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee in February 1997, and the committee never acted on it before the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Rep. Bob Stump introduced H.R. 736 on February 12, 1997, to repeal subtitle B of the Internal Revenue Code covering estate, gift, and generation-skipping taxes.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means on the day of introduction, which was its only committee action.
The bill had just one cosponsor and never received a hearing, markup, floor vote, or further action during the 105th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Heirs of very large estates are better off in the sense that no repeal took effect, so the estate tax on large inheritances remained in place; no one gained materially from the bill's failure, but concentrated wealth interests lost nothing either since the status quo was preserved by inaction rather than by a vote.

for.name: Rep. Bob Stump
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on February 12, 1997, and delivered introductory remarks.

for.name: Rep. Fox of Pennsylvania
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no further action, never scheduling a markup or advancing the bill.

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were Republicans, but no votes or recorded opposition ever occurred, so the partisan split cannot be measured.

industries.note: The estate tax falls only on the largest estates; full repeal would have eliminated it entirely, transferring tax liability on very large inheritances to the general taxpayer.
Repeal would reduce demand for estate-tax-driven planning services, though the effect is secondary and the industry also benefits from complexity that repeal would have eliminated.
